title: Blood, lymphatic and immune systems
note: hem/o and hemat/o mean blood, and -cyte means cell, so color roots name the blood cells: erythrocyte (red), leukocyte (white), thrombocyte (clotting). Count suffixes: -penia too few, -cytosis too many, -poiesis formation. Lymphatic and immune roots include lymph/o, lymphaden/o, splen/o, thym/o and immun/o.

read.title: Counting cells
text: Blood is a liquid tissue. About half of it is plasma, a straw-colored liquid that carries proteins, nutrients and clotting factors. The rest is formed elements, all arising in the red bone marrow through hematopoiesis. Each is named with -cyte, cell, and a color or function root. Erythrocytes, the red cells, carry oxygen bound to hemoglobin. Leukocytes, the white cells, defend the body; their types include neutrophils, eosinophils and lymphocytes. Thrombocytes, or platelets, are cell fragments that help form clots and stop bleeding, a process called hemostasis.

Laboratory results are often described with count suffixes. Add -penia when a count is low and -cytosis when it is high: thrombocytopenia is a low platelet count and leukocytosis is a high white cell count.

The lymphatic system returns tissue fluid, called lymph, to the blood and filters it through lymph nodes (lymphaden/o). The spleen (splen/o) filters blood, and the thymus (thym/o) is where T lymphocytes mature. Immune vocabulary rests on a simple pair: an antigen is anything that triggers an immune response, and an antibody is a protein that binds to a specific antigen.
